section_1.title: The Linear System as a Transformation
section_1.content: Introduce Ax = b by visualizing 'A' as a transformation of space. Before diving in, refresh the concept of a vector as a position. Show a 2D plane being 'warped' or 'stretched' by matrix A, turning a square grid into a new coordinate system.
section_1.example: Imagine a robot arm (the vector x) reaching for a target point (b). The matrix A represents the mechanical constraints of the arm's joints.

section_2.title: Column Space: Where can the Robot go?
section_2.content: Define the Column Space as the 'reachable territory.' If the columns of A are linearly dependent, the space collapses (e.g., from a plane to a line). Use a visual animation where the grid lines flatten into a line or point.
section_2.example: If a robot arm is stuck on a 2D table, its column space is the surface of the table. If the arm's joints 'lock' (linear dependence), the robot can only move along a single line.

section_3.title: Null Space: The 'Ghost' Inputs
section_3.content: Explain the Null Space as the set of vectors that 'disappear' into the origin (Ax = 0). Visually, this is the set of vectors that get squashed into a single point. This explains why some systems have multiple solutions.
section_3.example: A 'stealth mode' button on a device: Any input vector in the null space results in zero output (silence), making the device appear 'invisible' to the target.

section_4.title: Inverse Matrices: The 'Rewind' Button
section_4.content: Introduce the Inverse Matrix A⁻¹ as the geometric 'undo' operation. If A is a transformation, A⁻¹ maps the point b back to x. Emphasize that this only works if the transformation didn't collapse the space (i.e., det(A) ≠ 0).
section_4.example: A video game character moves from point A to point B. The inverse matrix is the 'Rewind' button that precisely retraces the path back to the starting position.

section_5.title: Summary and Synthesis
section_5.content: Bring it all together: A system has a unique solution if A is invertible (doesn't collapse space). If it collapses space, we either have infinite solutions (if b is in the column space) or no solution (if b is not).
section_5.example: Visual summary: A light projection. A = Lens (transformation), Column Space = The Image on the screen, Null Space = Rays hitting the same pixel, Inverse = Reconstructing the object from the image.
